title: Historical Phonology
full_title: Chinese Historical Phonology: The Sounds of Earlier Chinese
tagline: Why historical phonology matters, fanqie spellings, the *Qieyun* and *Guangyun*, the initials of Middle Chinese, its finals and tones, rhyme tables, Old Chinese, from Middle Chinese to Mandarin, and phonology for readers
summary: Chinese characters do not show how they sounded, yet poets rhymed and scholars recorded sounds for two thousand years. This course explains how the sounds of earlier Chinese are reconstructed: fanqie spellings, the rhyme dictionaries from the *Qieyun* to the *Guangyun*, the categories of Middle Chinese, the rhyme tables, the evidence for Old Chinese, and the changes that led to modern Mandarin — and shows how this knowledge helps in reading classical poetry and understanding the dialects.
overview: Why does 远上寒山石径斜 fail to rhyme in a schoolchild's reading, while a Cantonese speaker hears the rhyme instantly? Historical phonology — the discipline that reconstructs the sounds of earlier Chinese — answers with three strands of evidence: how ancient poems rhyme, what the fanqie spellings and rhyme dictionaries record, and how modern dialects and old Sino-Xenic loan strata correspond. This course teaches the craft rather than the pedigree.

We begin with fanqie spelling and the architecture of the Qieyun-Yunyun tradition (601 to 1008): its 193/206 rhyme divisions, initial classes, the divisions (等) and open/closed oppositions, and the four tones. We then read the Song rhyme tables that lay the whole system on a grid, and survey the great results of the Qing school and modern science: the fanqie connection method behind the recovery of the Qieyun initials, Old Chinese rhyme divisions from Chen Di and Gu Yanwu to Duan Yucai, and reconstruction from Karlgren, Wang Li and Li Fang-Kuei to Baxter-Sagart.

The last third is payoff: regular correspondences from Middle Chinese to Mandarin (redistribution of the entering tone, tone splitting by initial voicing, palatalization), how phonology serves the reading of classical poetry and the emendation of old texts, and what a modern learner can achieve with one table, one dictionary of reconstructions, and the exercises in this course.
outcomes: spell a character's traditional reading with fanqie and recover its initial and final from the two spelling characters
describe the architecture of the Qieyun/Yunyun system: 206 rhymes, rhyme groups (摄), divisions, open/closed, and the four tones
relate the 36 letters to the fanqie-connected initial classes and explain why the letters understate the system
read a page of a Song rhyme table and state what each cell encodes
summarize the main results of Qing Old-rhyme scholarship and modern reconstructions of Old and Middle Chinese
derive the regular correspondences from Middle Chinese to Mandarin (entering-tone distribution, tone splits, palatalization)
mark rhyme and tone-pattern in classical poetry and diagnose why a given line no longer rhymes today
use phonological evidence to adjudicate a textual crux or ambiguity in a classical passage

history.title: Qieyun
history.detail: Lu Fayan's rhyming handbook of 601, drawn from the conference of scholar-officials around Yan Zhitui, records the readings of 12,000-odd characters through fanqie spellings under 193 (later widened to 206) rhyme categories. The original is largely lost, but its skeleton lives in the Guangyun and in Dunhuang fragments — the foundation charter of Middle Chinese.

history.title: Guangyun
history.detail: The Song imperial revision Jingde Guangyun grew the Qieyun to some 26,000 characters under 206 rhymes with rich glosses; the only complete early rhyme book, it remains the primary ledger of Middle Chinese.

history.title: Yunjing
history.detail: The Mirror of Rhymes, the earliest fully surviving rhyme table, sets initials as columns, finals and divisions as rows, tones as strata — a phonological grid built without any alphabet.

history.title: Zhongyuan Yinyun
history.detail: Zhou Deqing's rhyming handbook for northern drama arranged common syllables into 586 homophone groups in the living spoken register: entering tone redistributed, level tone split, modern Mandarin taking shape on the page.

history.title: The Qing Old-rhyme school
history.detail: Building on Ming scholar Chen Di's rejection of ad-hoc rhyming readings, Gu Yanwu and then Duan Yucai partitioned the Odes' rhyme system (ten divisions, then seventeen) purely from internal evidence — the world's first rigorous distributional analysis.
history.people: 顾炎武、段玉裁 (Gu Yanwu, Duan Yucai)

history.title: Karlgren's reconstructions
history.detail: Bernhard Karlgren fused fanqie, rhyme tables, dialects and Tibetan-Sino-Xenic evidence into the first full value-system for Middle and Old Chinese, opening the international era — and the native corrections by Wang Li and Li Fang-Kuei.

history.title: Li Fang-Kuei's Old Chinese
history.detail: Li's studies of the Shuowen phonetic series turned the Qing rhyme divisions into an explanatory sound system — initials, clusters, vowels — published across the 1971-73 essays and still the methodological anchor.

history.title: Baxter-Sagart synthesis
history.detail: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction models a pre-Qin language with prefixation and sesquisyllabic rhythm, uniting rhyme behaviour, phonetic series, Sino-Tibetan comparison and transcriptions in one falsifiable system.

references.title: 《汉语音韵学讲义》
references.note: The standard university introduction: patient with fanqie drills, honest about contested points.

references.title: 《音韵学要纲》
references.note: Wang Li's compact classic; the framework of Middle Chinese and tone-splitting laws used by most textbooks descends from it.

references.title: Middle Chinese: A Study in Early Chinese Phonology
references.note: The best English-language treatment of the rhyme-table system and its phonological interpretation.

references.title: A Handbook of Old Chinese Phonology
references.note: The field's atlas of Old Chinese rhyme divisions and correspondences before the 2014 reconstruction.

references.title: 《李方桂全集》
references.note: Li Fang-Kuei's collected works — the anchor of modern reconstruction methodology in Chinese.

references.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction
references.note: The current international synthesis; read it side by side with the Qing masters for perspective.
